messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 48
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Social Ministry Worker
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 57

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Loss of Autonomy: Being forced to do something, Feeling Ill: Feeling physically unwell, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle, Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous, Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress
  Threat: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Negative Appraisals: Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Vignette:
Renée Marchand is a 48-year-old single woman of French-Canadian descent who works as a social ministry worker for a mid-sized urban parish, coordinating food assistance programs and connecting vulnerable community members with housing and health resources. She came to her first session carrying a canvas tote bag and a thermos of tea, and she sat in the chair closest to the office door without being directed to it. She had been referred by her parish priest, who had noticed that she was no longer making home visits.

Fourteen months ago, Renée was a passenger in a van being driven by a colleague after a late-evening community outreach event. A sedan ran a red light and struck the van on the passenger side — her side — at full speed. The impact rotated the vehicle across two lanes. Renée was conscious throughout. She described being pinned by a collapsed door frame, unable to move her left arm, unable to open her door, unable to do anything but wait while the smell of something burning reached her and other drivers stopped on the road. She was extracted by emergency responders after approximately twenty-two minutes. She sustained a fractured clavicle, three broken ribs, and a mild traumatic brain injury. Her colleague walked away with minor injuries. The driver of the sedan, who was uninsured, received no criminal charges. Renée was discharged from hospital after four days and was told, by medical staff and by the people who loved her, that she was lucky.

She did not feel lucky. In the weeks that followed, she found herself unable to accept rides from anyone, and within two months she had stopped attempting to drive herself as well. Her world contracted accordingly. The parish is three miles from her apartment, and she now walks or takes the subway, rerouting her path to avoid a particular intersection she passes in the van on the route she used to take. When she boards the subway, she moves immediately toward the doors and notes which end of the car is closest to the platform exit. She does the same in any enclosed space — the parish hall, the waiting rooms of the agencies she visits for clients, even the office where she now sits. She described this not as a habit but as a necessity, the way one might describe checking a smoke alarm. What frightened her most was not being able to get out. Being pinned in that crumpled door frame for twenty-two minutes had confirmed something she had begun to suspect: that when it mattered, her body would fail her and no one could reach her in time.

The physical aftermath of the accident has deepened this conviction. On days when she feels even mildly unwell — a headache, fatigue, the muscular tension that lingers in her left shoulder — she becomes acutely vigilant, interpreting each sensation as a signal that something worse is coming. She had come to believe that her body was no longer a reliable instrument, that it could betray her without warning, and so she had begun avoiding anything that might stress it further: she declined a colleague's invitation to a yoga class, stopped taking the stairs when she was tired, and cut short a dental appointment because the reclining chair made her feel too exposed and too still. She had also stopped allowing herself to rest fully. Lying on the sofa in the evening, she would find herself sitting upright within minutes, certain that relaxing her guard was precisely the condition under which something bad would happen.

At work, the consequences had become impossible to ignore. Home visits — the core of her role — require her to ride in a vehicle. She had rerouted her caseload twice, asking colleagues to cover visits without fully explaining why, and the parish coordinator had recently asked her directly whether she was managing. She had said yes. The lie had cost her something.

What finally brought her to seek help was a letter from the county informing her that the driver who struck the van had applied for a hardship exemption and would face no further civil liability. She read it three times at her kitchen table and then sat without moving for an hour. She had come to believe that what happened to her was not merely unlucky but wrong, that something corrective should have followed, and the letter confirmed that nothing would. She arrived at her first session not entirely sure what she was hoping for, but she said, quietly, that she wanted to stop feeling like the accident was still happening.
